item.title: Automatic geometric calibration and unwarping of rotating line-scan imaging systems using elliptical distortion of circular patterns
item.description:
The problem

A line-scan camera captures one line at a time, and motion supplies the second image dimension. How the image is formed therefore depends on that motion, and calibration has to describe it. Most line-scan calibration methods assume the object moves past the sensor in a straight line. Many inspection systems instead rotate the object: cylindrical workpieces, rotary surface profiling, panoramic imaging of rotationally symmetric parts. Each scan line is then taken at a different angle, a sector-scan (polar) geometry that distorts both the 2D intensity image and the 3D height profile. Calibration methods for rotating scanners typically rely on known angular motion, mechanical measurements or rotary encoders, which add complexity to the system.

The distortion itself carries the missing information. Under rotational scanning, the circular holes of a calibration plate appear as ellipses, and how the ellipses’ centres and aspect ratios change across the image encodes the rotation geometry. Earlier work used circular targets and ellipse fitting, but usually treated the deformation of the ellipses as a side effect of projection or misalignment, not as a record of the scanning geometry.

How it works

The method treats the image as polar data. A pixel’s column gives its distance from the rotation centre, r = x − xc, and its row gives the rotation angle, θ = k(y − yc), where k is the angular sampling rate in radians per row. The rotation centre (xc, yc) and k are unknown. All three are estimated from the ellipses in an image of a simple circular-hole plate, without encoders, mechanical measurements or auxiliary sensors. One polar-to-Cartesian mapping then corrects the 2D image and the 3D height map.

  1. Scan. The sensor stays still while the plate turns on a rotary stage. Each scan line becomes one image row at a new angle, so rows record angle and columns record distance from the rotation centre.
  2. Circles become ellipses. Under this sector-scan mapping, each round hole appears as an ellipse whose shape depends on its position. A single ellipse may be perturbed by noise, partial occlusion or imperfect edges, but together the ellipses follow stable trends, and the method estimates the calibration parameters from these collective trends rather than from any single precise measurement.
  3. Fit an ellipse to every hole. Hole regions are located (manually or automatically), segmented with an adaptive threshold, and their edges are refined to subpixel accuracy along the image gradient. After outlier edge points are removed, each contour is fitted with a direct least-squares ellipse fit. The centre and the aspect ratio ρi = rx,i / ry,i are recorded; ellipses with large residuals or unreasonable aspect ratios are rejected.
  4. Regress to find the rotation centre and sampling rate. The aspect ratio varies approximately linearly with the ellipse’s horizontal centre position, ρ = a·cx + b, so the rotation centre is where the line crosses zero, xc = −b/a. Because a small error in the slope a shifts xc strongly, the line is fitted robustly: RANSAC first removes gross outliers, then an iterative residual-based least-squares refinement (ILS) drops measurements with large residuals and refits, typically converging in 2–3 iterations. A linear regression on the vertical positions of the ellipse centres gives the angular sampling rate k.
  5. Unwarp. Each pixel of the corrected image is mapped back to the raw image with the estimated xc, yc and k, and its value is found by bilinear interpolation. The ellipses become circles again. For 3D data, each height value becomes a point X = r cos θ, Y = r sin θ, with its height Z unchanged. The laser profiler produces the 2D intensity image and the 3D height map from the same measurements, so one transformation corrects both.

Results

Rotation centre xc = −516.76 px with R² = 0.998 for the aspect-ratio regression, and angular sampling rate k = 0.00402 rad/pixel with residual angular error below 0.12° across all calibration holes (Section 4.4).
Circularity error ε from 0.21 ± 0.08 before unwarping to 0.02 ± 0.01 after, where ε = |rx − ry| / rx is 0 for a perfect circle (Section 4.5).
Standard deviation of xc: 0.5 px with ILS, against 1.4 px with RANSAC and 3.8 px with ordinary least squares (Table 3).

All experiments ran on a real system: a single industrial laser triangulation profiler (LPF2-050, OPT Machine Vision, 405 nm blue laser, 3,200 points per scan line) mounted above a programmable precision rotary stage. The profiler stays still while the calibration target rotates at constant speed, and it records the 2D intensity image and the 3D height profile from the same measurements. Three circular-hole calibration plates of different materials, metallic and ceramic, with different hole layouts, gave consistent estimates of the rotation centre and angular sampling parameters. Ellipse fitting reached an average RMS algebraic fitting error of 0.42 pixels. Unwarping restored the circular holes in the 2D image, and the same transformation reduced residual geometric distortion and improved the spatial regularity of the reconstructed 3D surfaces.

The estimate becomes more stable as more ellipses are used. Over 50 random repeats, the standard deviation of xc fell from 2.1 px with 5 ellipses to 0.6 px with 10 and 0.3 px with 20, and automatic detection with ILS also reached 0.3 px (Table 1). Spreading the ellipses widely across the field of view matters more than adding more of them: the paper recommends about 8–30 well-distributed ellipses covering at least 30–50% of the field of view. The method also stayed stable under simulated partial occlusion, salt-and-pepper and speckle noise, and defocus blur (Fig. 10). When the scanned angle exceeds about 10°, the regression is stable, with R² > 0.99 in most experiments.

The authors also state the method’s limits. The model assumes the rotation axis is perpendicular to the image plane and that the scan line passes through the centre of the calibration disk; axis tilt, wobble or a lateral offset of the scan line would need extra parameters. Very small scanned angles make the ellipses nearly circular, so xc and k become hard to observe. Strong lens distortion should be corrected first, and a warped or non-planar plate can bias the ellipse centres. For 3D data, the correction addresses distortion from the scanning geometry only; it does not model laser-plane calibration or focal-length variation.

item.title: Learning-based reconstruction of moving transparent objects
item.description:
This paper studies 3D reconstruction for moving transparent objects, a setting where refraction, weak surface texture, and motion make conventional structured-light reconstruction difficult.

This work appears in International Conference on Optoelectronic Science and Intelligent Sensing (SPIE), 1417511.

Algorithm principle

The method uses a learning-based reconstruction pipeline to compensate for the optical ambiguity of transparent objects and the temporal inconsistency caused by motion.

Visual material

Detailed method and result figures will be added when the original paper assets are available.

Results and impact

The work belongs to the structured-light and transparent-object reconstruction thread, where robustness matters for industrial surfaces that are glossy, transparent, or in motion.

item.title: OPT Projected Structured-Light 3D Cameras
item.description:
The projected structured-light series targets high-precision one-shot reconstruction without a motion platform. It is positioned for dimensional measurement, positioning, bin picking, semiconductor, 3C, lithium battery, and automotive component inspection.

Projected structured-light product matrix covering FPB and FPC series.

My role

My work focuses on the algorithm layer behind this product family: structured-light reconstruction, calibration, point-cloud cleanup, 2D/3D alignment, measurement tools, and Smart3 workflow integration for industrial deployment.

Principle

The camera projects encoded structured light onto the target, captures the deformed stripe or fringe pattern, and reconstructs 3D contour data through decoding, unwrapping, and geometric calibration. The product line is designed for rapid imaging and stable reconstruction under industrial production constraints.

Structured-light projection, encoded patterns, and 3D reconstruction.

Product strengths

The product family emphasizes one-shot imaging, no motion-platform requirement, hardware-side point-cloud output, high-quality projected stripes, multi-projector fusion, multi-exposure fusion, denoising, hole filling, and Smart3 deployment.

Dual projection and telecentric imaging

The high-precision dual-projector route reduces dead zones by projecting from multiple directions. The configuration is reported to reduce imaging blind spots by 95 percent and uses telecentric optics to improve edge stability and Z repeatability in macro measurement tasks.

Dual-projector point-cloud fusion reduces directional blind spots.

2D and 3D alignment

The structured-light products support pixel-level 2D/3D alignment so the same acquisition can serve recognition, defect localization, and 3D measurement. This is useful when classical measurement, AI detection, and point-cloud analysis need to share the same coordinate frame.

Pixel-aligned 2D and 3D output for inspection and measurement.

Applications

Typical applications include toothbrush or workpiece bin picking, headset and sidewall dispensing guidance, semiconductor pin inspection, sealing nail weld inspection, smartphone middle-frame inspection, and high-precision surface bump or dent detection.

One-shot 3D data supports segmentation and robot picking in unordered scenes.

item.title: 3D reconstruction of moving object by double sampling based on phase shifting profilometry
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) is one of the most commonly used 3D measurement techniques, valued for its high precision, robustness and full-field measurement. A projector casts at least three phase-shifted sinusoidal fringe patterns onto the object, and a camera views them from another angle. The object’s height distorts the fringes, and the 3D shape is computed from the phase of the deformed fringes and the system parameters. Because several images are needed, traditional PSP requires the object to stay static during reconstruction. Once it moves during fringe projection and capture, errors are introduced.

Earlier work tracks the object’s motion and compensates the resulting error, estimates the motion between the 3D data of adjacent frames, or uses a high-speed imaging system with shifted Gray code. One approach that estimates motion from the object’s start and end states is limited to uniform motion, and deep-learning methods that recover phase from a single fringe pattern need time-consuming network training and are hard to run in real time. The authors therefore look for a motion-error compensation method suited to real-time phase-shift measurement.

How it works

The method changes how the images are captured and how the phase is computed. The camera is triggered twice during every projected fringe pattern, so two images taken under the same fringe differ only by the object’s motion. With the motion known from tracking, a least-squares model recovers the object’s phase from three consecutive images, and overlapping groups of three images give one phase map each.

  1. Two shots per fringe. A trigger control device is added to the camera and projector. The projector projects N fringe images at a set rate and triggers the camera twice in each projection cycle: I11 and I12 are captured while fringe I1 is projected, I21 and I22 while I2 is projected, and so on.
  2. Separate motion from phase shift. Two images taken under the same projected fringe, such as I11 and I12, differ only by the phase shift caused by object motion (δ1 = 0). Images taken under different fringes also carry the PSP phase shift δ2 = 2π/N. The phase is analysed in I11, I12 and I21.
  3. Track the motion. The rotation matrix and translation vector describing the object’s motion are obtained by tracking the object. From them follows the coordinate transformation (fn, gn) that relates each point’s position before and after the motion.
  4. Solve for the phase by least squares. Each of the three images is written as A + B cos(ϕ + δk) + C sin(ϕ + δk), where ϕ is the reference-plane phase at the transformed coordinates. Minimising the squared error over the three images (N = 3) leads to a linear system D X = E with X = [A B C]T, and the phase change caused by the object is φ = tan−1(−C/B). The object is then reconstructed from the phase and the system parameters.
  5. Multiplex the images. Every three consecutive images give one object phase map, so the groups overlap and a new frame starts with each new image. Traditional PSP needs three projected patterns for each frame.

Results

Two images per projected fringe, captured through a trigger control device on the camera and projector (Section 3, Fig. 1).
One object phase map from every three consecutive images, by multiplexing the fringe images (Fig. 2, Fig. 5a).
Shooting frame rate doubled relative to the projector’s highest frame rate (Section 5).
Simulated object moving 10 pixels between fringe patterns: the proposed method reconstructs the block, while traditional PSP on the same images gives large errors (Figs. 5 and 6).

The method is verified by simulation. Fringe patterns are simulated for a static object and for an object that moves from left to right by 10 pixels between each two fringe patterns. For comparison, the static patterns are reconstructed with traditional PSP (Fig. 3 of the paper). In the moving case, images taken under the same projected fringe contain only the object’s motion, while images under different fringes contain both the fringe phase shift and the motion (Fig. 4 of the paper). The rotation matrix and translation vector of the motion are computed by tracking the object, the phase is computed with the proposed model, and with multiplexing every three images give an object phase map. These phase maps at different frames give a high-frame-rate 3D reconstruction of the moving block (Fig. 5). Traditional PSP applied to the same images shows large errors (Fig. 6).

In their conclusion, the authors note that the method only needs a newly derived formula and the projection of the first two fringe patterns of a three-step phase shift to reconstruct the moving object, and that it doubles the shooting frame rate at low cost without losing the advantages of PSP. The comparison with traditional PSP is shown visually in Figs. 5 and 6.

item.title: 3D reconstruction of the moving object with double-shooting based on phase shifting profilometry
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) is one of the most commonly used 3D measurement techniques, valued for its high accuracy, robustness and full-field measurement. A projector casts at least three phase-shifted sinusoidal fringe patterns onto the object, and a camera views them from another angle. The object’s height distorts the fringes, the phase of the fringes describes that distortion, and the phase plus the system parameters give the 3D shape. Because several patterns are used, traditional PSP requires the object to stay still: if it moves while the patterns are projected and captured, measurement errors appear.

Frame rate is a second limit. A projector typically shows 8-bit fringe patterns at up to 120 Hz, while a camera easily exceeds 1000 Hz, so the frame rate of the reconstructed point clouds is limited by the projector. Defocusing a projector that shows binary patterns can exceed 1000 Hz, but the amount of defocus is hard to control and quantify, and high-speed cameras and projectors raise the cost considerably. The paper asks how to reconstruct moving objects at a high frame rate with low-cost equipment.

How it works

A trigger controller is added between the camera and the projector, so the camera captures each projected fringe pattern twice and collects more fringe information about the moving object. The paper then analyses how the object’s motion changes the phase across three consecutive images, builds a fringe model that includes the motion, extracts the phase under this mixed phase shift, and reuses the captured images to obtain more reconstructed frames.

  1. Double shooting. The projector shows its N phase-shifted patterns at its normal rate, and the camera is triggered twice within each projection period. Every projected pattern therefore yields two camera images of the moving object.
  2. Mixed phase shift. Two images taken under the same pattern differ only by the phase shift caused by the object’s motion. Images taken under different patterns contain this motion-induced shift as well as the ordinary PSP phase shift. For three images I1, I2, I3, the shifts are δ1 = δ2 = 0 and δ3 = 2π/N.
  3. Fringe model with motion. An object motion tracking algorithm computes the rotation–translation matrix that describes the object’s motion. It gives the coordinate transform (fn, gn) between images, and each image is written as In = a + B cos hn + C sin hn, with hn = ϕ(fn, gn) + δn, where ϕ is the phase of the reference plane.
  4. Least-squares phase. For each pixel, a, B and C are found by minimising the squared difference between the model and the captured images. Since B = cos φ and C = −sin φ, the phase change caused by the object’s shape is φ = arctan(−C / B).
  5. Image reuse. The captured images are reused: every three adjacent images give one frame of object phase, whereas traditional PSP builds each frame from its own group of images. This raises the reconstruction frame rate of the moving object while the projector speed stays limited.

Results

Mean error on the moving object: 0.1575 mm with traditional PSP, 0.0344 mm with the proposed method (Table 1).

The experimental system consists of an industrial camera (OPT-CC1-048A-RM-G, 1800 × 1600 pixels), a projector (TJ-S50, 1280 × 720 pixels) and a motorised translation stage. The measured object is a mask. The camera runs at 20 frames/s, the stage moves at 20 mm/s, and the field of view is 70 mm × 80 mm. The mask is first reconstructed at rest with traditional PSP, and this result serves as ground truth for the error evaluation. On the moving stage, the two images taken under one projected pattern contain only the object’s motion, while images under different patterns contain both motion and fringe phase shift. The rotation–translation matrix comes from an object motion tracking algorithm, and every three adjacent images give one phase map. The proposed method reconstructs the moving mask, whereas traditional PSP applied to the moving object shows large errors.

The authors name the accuracy of the object tracking algorithm as the most important limitation: it directly sets the reconstruction accuracy, and existing tracking algorithms have difficulty describing large motions. The method can only reconstruct objects undergoing 2D translation; because of the limits of motion tracking, it cannot handle 2D rotation or 3D motion. It does not require the object to move at constant speed, but the camera must capture clear fringe images of the moving object.
